links.note: Canon 1 of the Council of Constantinople (381) anathematized the Semi-Arians, called Pneumatomachi, by name. A law of 383 also banned assemblies of Eunomians, Arians, Macedonians and Pneumatomachi. In 451 the Council of Chalcedon said the creed of 381 set out the faith on the Holy Spirit against those who denied his sovereignty.

sources.work: Council of Constantinople (381), Canon 1
sources.quote: and that of the Semi-Arians or Pneumatomachi, and that of the Sabellians, and that of the Marcellians, and that of the Photinians, and that of the Apollinarians.

sources.work: Codex Theodosianus 16.5.11 (law of 25 July 383)
sources.quote: omnes omnino, quoscumque diversarum haeresum error exagitat, id est eunomiani, arriani, macedoniani, pneumatomachi manichaei, encratitae, apotactitae, saccofori, hydroparastatae nullis circulis coeant,

sources.work: Council of Chalcedon (451), Definition of Faith (NPNF 2.14)
sources.quote: which doctrine they declared unto all men, not as though they were introducing anything that had been lacking in their predecessors, but in order to explain through written documents their faith concerning the Holy Ghost against those who were seeking to destroy his sovereignty.

drafter_flags: The creed of 381 is first attributed to that council in the acts of Chalcedon (451); the Chalcedon source is cited for exactly that.
links.change_reason: Old link sound (quotes re-checked). Added Chalcedon's Definition, the earliest vendored text tying the creed's article on the Spirit to this party, so the legacy sentence ('the third article is the answer to this party') has a source on the link.

links.note: Ulfila, bishop of the Goths, took part in the council at Constantinople in 360 that confirmed the Homoian creed. In 427 or 428 the Homoian bishop Maximinus came to Africa with the Goths and named the creed of Ariminum as his faith. In the fifth century the historian Socrates wrote that many Goths still held it.

sources.work: Sozomen, Church History IV.24 (trans. Hartranft, NPNF 2.2)
sources.quote: invited thither several bishops of Bithynia, among whom were Maris, bishop of Chalcedon, and Ulfilas, bishop of the Goths.

sources.work: Socrates, Church History II.41 (trans. Zenos, NPNF 2.2)
sources.quote: To this creed Ulfilas bishop of the Goths gave his assent, although he had previously adhered to that of Nicæa;

sources.work: Possidius, Life of Augustine 17, quoted in the editors' admonition to the Collatio cum Maximino (PL 42)
sources.quote: Cum ipsorum quoque Arianorum episcopo quodam Maximino cum Gothis ad Africam veniente,apud Hipponem

sources.work: Collatio cum Maximino Arianorum episcopo 1 (Maximinus's own answer; PL 42, Migne 1886 printing)
sources.quote: teneo fidem que Arimini! a trecentis et triginta episcopis, non solum exposita, sed etiam subscri- ptionibus firmata est.

sources.work: Maurist editors' admonition to the Collatio cum Maximino (PL 42), on its date
sources.quote: videlicet aut 427, aut 428.

sources.work: Socrates, Church History IV.33 (trans. Zenos, NPNF 2.2)
sources.quote: Therefore it is that so many of the Goths are even to the present time infected with the errors of Arianism, they having on the occasion preferred to become adherents to that heresy on the emperor’s account.

links.named_in_text: homoian longDescription and why (Ulfila's mission; Goths, Vandals and Lombards in this form; Homoian kingdoms). The Gothic entry's own summary also names it ('Descended from Ulfila's missionary church').
drafter_flags: 'Continued as' is an interpretation; it is graded Documented because Socrates (fifth century) and Maximinus (427) show the same Gothic Homoian church and creed still standing after Ulfila. No repo-cited secondary work states the continuity, so it could not be Widely Accepted on a consensus reading.

The two entries overlap in date (Homoian 4th-6th c.; Gothic 451-c. 680). The Homoian entry's own text runs to Toledo 589 and the Lombards. Reviewer may want the Homoian entry's dates cut to the 4th-5th c. so the period split is clean; that is the entry owner's call.
The Maximinus quote is raw OCR from PL 42 ('Arimini!', 'subscri- ptionibus'), copied as it stands. Kauffmann 1899 cites the same words (line 3224) in a cleaner hand.
Socrates's own phrase is 'infected with the errors of Arianism'; the note uses neutral wording.
links.change_reason: New. The Homoian text names Ulfila's Gothic church and the Homoian kingdoms, which the census carries on as the era-3 Gothic entry; no link joined them.

links.note: The emperor Constantius II called the bishops to two councils in 359, hoping to bring them all to one creed. A council at Constantinople in 360 confirmed the creed read at Ariminum, and Ulfila of the Goths signed it. In 427 or 428 the Homoian bishop Maximinus still named that creed as his faith.

sources.quote: The emperor’s object in these arrangements was to effect a general unity of opinion;

links.named_in_text: homoian relationsSummary ('the imperial church itself'), longDescription and why (backed by Constantius II and Valens, adopted at the councils of 359 and 360)
drafter_flags: Type choice needs a reviewer's eye. The relationship is imperial sponsorship: the Homoian creed was set at councils the emperor called. None of the six types names that. 'Influenced' fits the evidence that the Homoians kept the imperial councils' creed as their own (Ulfila 360, Maximinus 427). 'Gave rise to' would claim more; 'in contact with' would claim less than the sources show.

The pair already has an 'argued against' link (the Theodosian church of 381 against the Homoians). Both are true at different dates; the census treats the imperial church of 312-451 as one entry, so it is on both sides of the Homoian story.
Valens's backing (Socrates IV.1, npnf202 lines 12262-12264: 'in his anxiety to promote the Arian cause') is verified but left out of the note to keep it to three sentences.
links.change_reason: New. The Homoian text's central claim, that it was for a time the imperial church's position, had no link.

links.note: In his Dialogue against the Luciferians, written about 379, Jerome blames the Homoian leaders Valens and Ursacius for the council of Ariminum. There, he says, the Nicene faith was condemned, and the whole world groaned to find itself Arian.

sources.work: Jerome, Dialogue against the Luciferians 19 (trans. Fremantle, NPNF 2.6)
sources.quote: began to wave their palms, and to say they had not denied that He was a creature, but that He was like other creatures.

sources.work: Jerome, Dialogue against the Luciferians 19 (trans. Fremantle, NPNF 2.6)
sources.quote: At that moment the term Usia was abolished: the Nicene Faith stood condemned by acclamation. The whole world groaned, and was astonished to find itself Arian.

sources.work: W. H. Fremantle, introduction to Jerome's Dialogue against the Luciferians (NPNF 2.6)
sources.quote: This Dialogue was written about 379,

links.named_in_text: homoian longDescription and why (Jerome's line that the world groaned to find itself Arian)
drafter_flags: The NPNF introduction dates the Dialogue 'about 379' (npnf206 line 31412), three years before the Jerome entry's window opens (c. 382). Reviewer may judge that this belongs to Jerome before his circle formed and drop the link; the Homoian text uses Jerome as a witness, not as a party.
The Dialogue is aimed at the Luciferians; its attack on Valens and Ursacius is a passage within it, not its purpose. The names are in the passage itself (32403-32409, with an editor's note between).
links.change_reason: New. The Homoian text quotes Jerome; his passage condemns the Homoian leaders by name.

links.note: Theodoret, writing in the fifth century, says Bishop Leontius of Antioch made Aetius a deacon. Two ascetics of the city, Flavian and Diodore, protested in public that this disgraced the church. Leontius then suspended Aetius.

sources.work: Theodoret, Church History II.19 (trans. Jackson, NPNF 2.3)
sources.quote: At this juncture Aetius, the master of Eunomius, who promoted the Arian error by his speculations, was admitted to the diaconate.

sources.work: Theodoret, Church History II.19 (trans. Jackson, NPNF 2.3)
sources.quote: Flavianus and Diodorus, however, who had embraced an ascetic career, and were open champions of the Apostolic decrees, publicly protested against the attacks of Leontius against true religion.

sources.work: Theodoret, Church History II.19 (trans. Jackson, NPNF 2.3)
sources.quote: That a man nurtured in iniquity and scheming to win notoriety by ungodliness should be counted worthy of the diaconate, was, they urged, a disgrace to the Church.

links.named_in_text: anomoean longDescription and why (Aetius, a deacon at Antioch). Diodore is named in the Antiochene entry's own text as Chrysostom's teacher.
drafter_flags: The anomoean text names Antioch, not Diodore's circle; the inventory proposed 'in contact with'. The source shows a protest aimed at Aetius by name, so 'argued against' is the better type.
Theodoret is a later Antiochene writer and partial to Flavian and Diodore. Socrates's editor cites the same story from Theodoret (npnf202, 8480-8486), not from an independent source.
links.change_reason: New. Documents the Antiochene opposition to Aetius that the anomoean text's 'deacon at Antioch' points to.

prose_changes.old: The Homoians — from the Greek homoios, "like" — taught that the Son is like the Father according to the Scriptures, and refused to go further and call him of one being with the Father, on the grounds that Scripture never used the word and no council should force it on anyone; they did not call themselves Arians, and that label came from opponents who wanted them tied to a man most of them had never followed.
prose_changes.new: The Homoians — from the Greek homoios, "like" — taught that the Son is like the Father according to the Scriptures. They refused to go further and call him of one being with the Father, because Scripture never used the word and no council should force it on anyone. They did not call themselves Arians; that label came from their opponents. One of their own bishops put it the other way round: Arius had followed the bishops, not the bishops Arius.
prose_changes.reason: Split a 70-word sentence. The Homoian side's own words now carry the claim: Auxentius 48 (Kauffmann 1899, lines 15174-15176, the Son 'like' the Father 'secundum diuinas scribturas') and Maximinus's commentary (line 14834, 'constat ergo Arrium episcopos secutum fuisse, non episcopos Arrium'). The motive clause 'who wanted them tied to a man most of them had never followed' had no source and is dropped.

prose_changes.old: Through that mission the Goths, Vandals, Burgundians, and Lombards became Christians in this form, and Homoian kingdoms ruled Italy, Spain, and North Africa for generations after the empire itself had turned Nicene — the Visigoths of Spain going over to the Nicene creed at Toledo in 589, with the Lombards of Italy the last to follow, two generations later.
prose_changes.new: The Goths became Christians in this form, and the Vandals, Burgundians, and Lombards held it too. Jordanes, a sixth-century historian of the Goths, says they passed it on to "all people of their speech." Homoian kingdoms ruled Italy, Spain, and North Africa for generations after the empire itself had turned Nicene. The Visigoths of Spain went over to the Nicene creed at Toledo in 589, and the Lombards of Italy were the last to follow, two generations later.
prose_changes.reason: 'Through that mission' made Ulfila's own mission the cause of the Vandal, Burgundian and Lombard conversions; no vendored text says so. Socrates IV.33 credits Valens and Fritigern for the Goths, and Jordanes 25.133 (lines 1655-1659) says the Visigoths spread it to the Ostrogoths, Gepids and 'all people of their speech'. Each people's Homoian faith is attested: Vandals (Victor of Vita, 1605 trans., line 2), Burgundians (Gregory of Tours, Brehaut 1916, line 2102), Lombards (Paul the Deacon IV.42, lines 9051-9053, Rothari still Arian, d. 652). Toledo 589 in the vendored Toledo III acts. Long sentence split.

prose_changes.old: Its bishop Ulfila spent his life among the Goths, made an alphabet for their language, and translated the Bible into it, so that the Goths, Vandals, Burgundians, and Lombards all became Christians in this form, and Homoian kingdoms ruled Italy, Spain, and North Africa for generations after the empire itself had turned Nicene.
prose_changes.new: Its bishop Ulfila spent his life among the Goths, made an alphabet for their language, and translated the Bible into it. The Goths became Christians in this form, and the Vandals, Burgundians, and Lombards held it too. Homoian kingdoms ruled Italy, Spain, and North Africa for generations after the empire itself had turned Nicene.
prose_changes.reason: Same fix as the long description: 'so that' made Ulfila's translation the cause of four peoples' conversion, which no vendored text supports. Long sentence split.

prose_changes.old: Ulfila's Gothic Bible is the foundation document of Germanic philology — the earliest substantial writing in any Germanic language. And the great silver-and-gold copy of it made for Theoderic's court survives in Uppsala.
prose_changes.new: Large parts of Ulfila's Gothic Bible survive, and scholars of the Germanic languages still edit and study it. Its finest copy, written in silver and gold letters on purple parchment in the fifth or sixth century, is kept in Uppsala.
prose_changes.reason: Streitberg's edition (wulfila_gothic-bible-v1-got_streitberg1908.txt, lines 1348-1353) places the Codex Argenteus in Uppsala and dates it 5th/6th century, silver and gold on purple, but says nothing of Theoderic's court; no vendored or repo-cited source does. 'Foundation document' and 'earliest substantial writing' have no vendored or repo-cited source either; both are wanted.

prose_changes.old: Its buildings survive too: the Arian Baptistery and Sant'Apollinare Nuovo in Ravenna were built for Homoian worship, and their mosaics are among the finest anywhere.
prose_changes.new: Its buildings survive too. Ravenna was the capital of Theoderic, an Arian king, and its Arian Baptistery and Sant'Apollinare Nuovo still stand, with mosaics among the finest anywhere.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored text says these buildings were built for Homoian worship (Agnellus's Liber Pontificalis of Ravenna is not vendored). Theoderic's Arian faith is in Hodgkin's introduction to the Variae (cassiodorus_variae-letters-hodgkin1886.txt, line 1848). Agnellus is wanted.

prose_changes.old: The clauses most Christians recite each week were sharpened precisely to close the space this tradition tried to hold open.
prose_changes.new: In 381 the Council of Constantinople confirmed the faith of Nicaea, which calls the Son of one being with the Father. In the same canon it condemned the Homoians by name, as "the Arians or Eudoxians."
prose_changes.reason: The creed's key clause dates from 325, before the Homoian party formed (359-360), so 'sharpened precisely' against them is not right. What is documented: Constantinople 381, canon 1, confirms the Nicene faith and anathematizes 'the Arians or Eudoxians' (npnf214, lines 13971-13976, 13985-13987).

prose_changes.old: The radical wing of the fourth-century Arian controversy, and a different party from the Homoians it is usually filed with - the two split at Constantinople in 360.
prose_changes.new: The radical wing of the fourth-century Arian controversy, and a different party from the Homoians it is usually filed with. The break began at Constantinople in 360, when a Homoian council deposed Aetius.
prose_changes.reason: The sources do not put the whole split in 360. The Homoian council of 360 deposed Aetius (Sozomen IV.24; its own letter in Theodoret II.24), but Eunomius stayed with Eudoxius for a time (Theodoret II.25); Socrates IV.13 and Philostorgius IX.4 put the final break under Valens.

prose_changes.old: The party split from the Homoians at Constantinople in the same year, when the Homoian creed was imposed and Aetius exiled - which is why filing the two together misreads the controversy.
prose_changes.new: The break with the Homoians began at Constantinople in the same year, when their council confirmed the Homoian creed and deposed Aetius. Within a few years Eunomius and Aetius had broken away entirely, so filing the two parties together misreads the controversy.
prose_changes.reason: As the summary: 360 is the start of the break, not all of it. Theodoret II.25 dates Eunomius's own sect to after his flight from Cyzicus (c. 361); Socrates IV.13 and Philostorgius IX.4 to Valens's reign. 'Within a few years' covers both.

prose_changes.old: Their opponents called them Pneumatomachians, Spirit-fighters, and attached to them the name of Macedonius, a deposed bishop of Constantinople, on evidence later writers found thin.
prose_changes.new: Their opponents called them Pneumatomachians, Spirit-fighters. The historian Socrates named them after Macedonius, a deposed bishop of Constantinople, but he also says the party was named after Marathonius of Nicomedia.
prose_changes.reason: 'Later writers found thin' has no vendored or repo-cited source. Socrates II.45 (npnf202, lines 9817-9837) names Macedonius, reports the rival name 'Marathonians', and says the homoousians called them Pneumatomachi.

prose_changes.old: Basil's method in arguing it, appealing to the church's practice of prayer and baptism as evidence of what it believes, became a standing move in Christian theology long after the opponents it was aimed at had gone.
prose_changes.new: Basil argued it in a way of his own. He took the church's practice of prayer and baptism as evidence of what it believes.
prose_changes.reason: Basil's method is documented (On the Holy Spirit 67, npnf208 lines 14130-14140: 'as we are baptized, so also under the obligation to believe'). No vendored or repo-cited source shows it becoming 'a standing move' in later theology; a reception study is wanted.

prose_changes.old: It was condemned at Rome in 377 and again by name at Constantinople in 381.
prose_changes.new: It was condemned at a council in Rome in the 370s, and again by name at Constantinople in 381.
prose_changes.reason: The Roman council's year is disputed: the NPNF note to Sozomen VI.25 gives 377 (Rade) and 374 (Hefele) (npnf202, lines 39029-39031).

prose_changes.old: Condemned at Rome in 377 and by name at Constantinople in 381, Apollinaris's own writings survived mostly because his followers kept circulating them under other men's names.
prose_changes.new: His teaching was condemned at Rome in the 370s and by name at Constantinople in 381. His own writings survived mostly because his followers kept circulating them under other men's names.
prose_changes.reason: Same date fix. The opening phrase also attached the condemnation to his writings rather than to him. The forged names are in Lietzmann 1904, lines 5478-5481 (Leontius on works passed off under Gregory Thaumaturgus, Athanasius and Julius).

prose_changes.old: The question he raised is the one Ephesus and Chalcedon spent the next century answering.
prose_changes.new: The question he raised, how much of a human being Christ became, ran on into the councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon.
prose_changes.reason: 'Spent the next century answering' overstates: Ephesus and Chalcedon answered Nestorius and Eutyches. What links them to Apollinaris is documented: both affirm Christ's rational soul (Cyril's letter read at Ephesus, npnf214 lines 15669-15677 and 15737; Chalcedon's Definition, lines 20280-20282).

prose_changes.old: The controversy also set the terms for the next century: Ephesus in 431 and Chalcedon in 451 are both, in part, continued work on the question of how much humanity Christ took.
prose_changes.new: The controversy also shaped the next century. At Ephesus in 431 the bishops heard Cyril's letter saying the Word took flesh "animated by a rational soul." At Chalcedon in 451 they defined Christ as truly man, with a rational soul and a body.
prose_changes.reason: Replaces an interpretive frame with what the councils' texts say: Ephesus, Session I, reads Cyril's letter (npnf214 lines 15669-15677; 'flesh animated by a rational soul', 15737); Chalcedon's Definition, 'of a reasonable soul and [human] body' (20280-20282).

A repo-cited modern work on the Codex Argenteus and Theoderic's court, if that attribution is to come back

A vendored text or repo-cited study on the Macedonius attribution, if the old 'evidence later writers found thin' is to come back
escalations: Link-type gap, flagged not decided: imperial sponsorship of a creed (Constantius and the Homoian councils of 359-360) fits none of the six types cleanly. I drafted 'influenced' (imperial-juridical-christianity--homoian-arian-christianity--2). If the reviewer thinks this needs a new type or a ruling, that is a method change for Mark.

Entry overlap, for the owner: homoian-arian-christianity (4th-6th c.) and gothic-and-vandal-homoian-christianity (451-c. 680) cover the same kingdoms and endings. The new 'continued as' link assumes a period split; the Homoian text's last third duplicates the Gothic entry.

Candidate link found, not drafted (no text names it): Auxentius 48 (Kauffmann 1899, 15174-15176) has Ulfila rejecting the 'Macedonian' reading of 'like', and the homoian side's attack on the homoousians ('Homousianorum sectam destruebat'). A homoian-arian-christianity argued-against link to pneumatomachian-current may be worth a later pass.

Coordinator note (1): the homoian text does not name the Council of Aquileia, so no disposition points to group C's link. The Homoian reply is vendored, though: Maximinus's commentary defending Palladius (Kauffmann 1899, from line 14829). It would support a separate homoian-arian-christianity argued-against link to the Aquileian or Ambrosian entry if either text names it. Left for the merge.

Unsourced reception language left in place, flagged: anomoean legacy ('the Cappadocian theology that the Nicene tradition still uses' is supported by Basil Letter 234 for its content, not its later use) and apollinarian legacy ('still quoted in arguments that have nothing to do with Apollinaris').
